# Draft:Battle of Geli Zakho (1962)

Kurdistan Democratic Party (PDK) / Peshmerga
| combatant2 =  Iraqi Army (2nd Battalion of the 3rd Brigade)
| commander1 = Isa Suwar, Mullah Salih Haji Balqusi, Ali Halo
| commander2 = Colonel Majid Saba al-Abusi, Colonel Mohammed Yahya
| strength1 = Several hundred Peshmerga divided into six groups
| strength2 = 1 regiment, 35 vehicles including 5 tanks and support vehicles
| casualties1 = 3 killed (Yasin Merozi, Sabri Abdi, Qadir Ismail Hassan), several wounded
| casualties2 = 6 officers + 173 soldiers captured, 53 wounded, regimental commander wounded; all weapons, ammunition, vehicles, and equipment seized

The Battle of Geli Zakho was a key engagement during the Kurdish struggle against the Iraqi government in the early 1960s. The battle was part of the broader Kurdish–Iraqi conflicts during the Aylul Revolution.
Background
Prior to the battle, the Peshmerga had taken control of several government outposts and established positions in Turkzha and Qalma villages in the Geli Zakho and Slivana districts. The Kurdistan Democratic Party (PDK) maintained covert networks within the Iraqi army, allowing the timely transmission of intelligence to Peshmerga commanders. On 1 April 1962, the Peshmerga received information that a military regiment from Sheikhan, commanded by Colonel Majid Saba al-Abusi, was moving to replace the Batifa Regiment. This intelligence enabled the Peshmerga to plan a coordinated ambush.
Battle
The Peshmerga forces organized into six groups with specific objectives, including blocking military checkpoints, cutting telephone lines between Zakho and Mosul to prevent reinforcements, and attacking the main convoy of the regiment. Camouflaged with tree leaves and positioned along ambush sites, the Peshmerga launched their assault as the convoy reached the end of the gorge in Geli Zakho.
The engagement resulted in significant Iraqi losses: 6 officers and 173 soldiers were captured, 53 were wounded, and the Peshmerga seized all weapons, ammunition, vehicles, and equipment. Among the Peshmerga, 3 fighters were killed (Yasin Merozi, Sabri Abdi, Qadir Ismail Hassan) and several others were wounded.
Aftermath
The victory had major political and military consequences. High-ranking Iraqi officials hesitated to report the defeat to President Abdul Karim Qasim due to the embarrassment caused. The battle demonstrated the growing strength and organization of the Kurdish resistance and indicated that the government could not easily suppress the Kurdish movement. In response, the Iraqi military intensified operations, deployed additional troops, and carried out arrests and expulsions targeting civilians and alleged Kurdish supporters, particularly in Zakho.
